Stories / Montréal · Quebec · Versailles · 1759–1760

Story · Seven Years’ War, 18th century

Montréal, 1759–1760: “the loss of the colony”, Vaudreuil writes in cipher to the minister

April 1759: New France expects attack on three fronts, Lake Champlain, the Great Lakes and the St Lawrence. The governor general, Pierre de Rigaud de Vaudreuil, writes to the Navy minister, entirely in cipher, what he cannot say in clear: the famine, his plan, and the quarrel with Montcalm. Sixteen months later, three weeks before the capitulation of Montréal, he writes again. None of these four letters has ever been printed.

A story by Brice Dudout · reading with Claude · documents: Archives nationales d’outre-mer (Aix-en-Provence), COL C11A 104 and 105; key: COL C11E 10 · published 14 November 2026

“The loss of the colony has been regarded as quite evident; the measures I take for its preservation have been criticised by certain officers of the land troops.”

Vaudreuil to the minister, Montréal, 10 April 1759, “for you alone” (ciphered passage, read with the 1757 table; our translation).

What is new, what was known

Known. The fall of Quebec (September 1759) and of Montréal (September 1760), and the discord between Vaudreuil and Montcalm, are among the most studied episodes of Canadian history.[3] The four letters are in Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue (nos. 1388–1391), which pointed to the 1757 table as a lead.[2] In June 1759 the Navy office summarised three of them in a few lines, printed in 1858.[4]

What we add, as far as we know. (1) The text of the three letters of April 1759, never printed: read, 99.6%, 97.7% and 99.5% of words certain or probable. (2) The letter of 13 August 1760, read in part (91.8%). (3) What Vaudreuil told the minister alone about Montcalm. Daniel Bourdeau read these letters on his side, on the same day, with the same table; the two readings sit side by side in his repository.[2]

April 1759: famine and the plan

The winter had been terrible. On 8 April Vaudreuil describes the ration cut to four ounces of bread a day, the cattle and horses nearly all eaten; he has already taken the millers’ dues and the curés’ tithes. He has had the militia counted: 6,356 men for Quebec, 5,455 for Montréal, 1,313 for Trois-Rivières. He expects the British everywhere: at Carillon, on the Belle-Rivière (Fort Duquesne has been evacuated and destroyed), at Niagara, at La Présentation, and before Quebec.

“All things considered, I see the same plan reborn that the Duke of Cumberland conceived. General Hamerts, who was his aide-de-camp, doubtless wants to make good General Braddock’s failure. Quebec too is threatened by forces incomparably greater than all those of this colony.”

“Hamerts” is Amherst, spelt as heard. On 16 April Vaudreuil returns to provisions: if the supply ships are taken at sea, let the contractor have them replaced by his correspondents in France; a supplement is needed, “without it it would fall of itself”.

“For you alone”: Montcalm

The letter of 10 April encloses the memorandum in which Montcalm sets out his reflections on the campaign, with Vaudreuil’s answers; these enclosures have been in print since 1891.[5] The letter itself, in cipher, says what the enclosures do not: Montcalm’s view that the colony is lost “has been the talk of the officer, the townsman and the soldier”, and has spread “through all the parishes”. Vaudreuil threatens to send back to France the officers who speak against him, but handles the general with care:

“In short I am doing everything to avoid the scandal of a rupture between him and me. I consider only the good of the service itself and the glory of His Majesty’s arms.”

He gives him command of the army at Carillon. In July Niagara capitulates; on 13 September Montcalm is mortally wounded before Quebec, which surrenders on the 18th.[3]

August 1760: “masters of our waters”

The last letter is written from Montréal on 13 August 1760. The British are coming up the river; they number about 40,000; Murray is turning the Canadians and discrediting the bills of exchange; only ten thousand pounds of powder are left.

“We are without a navy or anything like one. The English are masters of our waters; they can go wherever they like on the river.”

Vaudreuil hopes the frigate Machault has run the blockade at the Restigouche. He does not know it, but she no longer exists: on 8 July her commander had scuttled her so that her cargo would not be taken.[6] Montréal capitulates on 8 September 1760.

The entry, text and translation →

Vaudreuil’s cipher

  • A nomenclator of 700 numbers: syllables, words, names, letters with two homophones, set out in ten-by-ten tables per hundred, with no word division.
  • The period table survives: “Chiffre avec M. le Mis de Vaudreuil, Gouverneur et Lieutenant général de la Nouvelle-France”, 1757, enciphering and deciphering tables (ANOM C11E 10, ff. 285–290v).[1]
  • A working cipher: the same table serves from April 1759 to August 1760.

How we read it

  1. The 1757 table was transcribed and frozen by SHA-256 hash before any measurement, with a protocol written and hashed in advance.
  2. A held-out measurement on another letter of Vaudreuil, of 8 May 1759, an old copy of which gives the cipher groups with the period decipherment between the lines: over 1,134 groups, agreement 0.972 with that decipherment, against at best 0.185 for 200 shuffled tables (thresholds set in advance: 0.85, and 0.30 above the best control).
  3. The reading of the four letters, with 20 values corrected from context, never applied to the measurement.
  4. The count, under Daniel Bourdeau’s rule (95% of words read by sense): 8 April, 2,003 words of 2,012; 10 April, 676 of 692; 16 April, 209 of 210; 13 August 1760, 1,314 of 1,431.

What remains uncertain

  • The letter of 13 August 1760 has 94 groups cut by the binding; we restore about 90 from sense, and the rule does not count them: read in part. Daniel Bourdeau counts it at 93.3%.
  • A single reader of the numbers: agents (Claude), on enlarged images; no human re-reading on the images yet.
  • Prior work. Printed sources checked on 5 November 2026 (Casgrain, Lévis collection, 12 vols.; É. Richard’s calendar of ANOM F3; RAPQ 1920–1923; Canadian Archives reports; Parkman and others): no text of these letters. Rechecked on 14 November (Daniel Bourdeau’s repository, web search). Also on 14 November: the RAPQ 1920–1942 searched in full text (the 1924–1927 volumes are missing on Internet Archive), and full-text searches of BAnQ numérique, with a positive control, and of Canadiana: no text of these letters. Not on DECODE according to Daniel Bourdeau’s survey.
  • No image: the images of Library and Archives Canada carry no open licence; they are not reproduced. The illustration is a schematic of places, not an accurate map.
